newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Cocoa, sugar likely to build on gain.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Cocoa, sugar likely to build on gain.

text.p: London's cocoa and white sugar futures markets are expected to maintain upward momentum this week and build on the recent bullish tone, traders and analysts said on Monday.
But robusta coffee, while still looking bullish in the longer term amid seasonal fears of Brazilian frost, might consolidate and possibly edge lower, they said.
London traders said they expected robusta futures to move in a range this week with a slight downside bias.
Technically, analysts expected September coffee to ratchet lower in the near term to test support near $1,600 a tonne, the base from which it rallied to 20-month highs.
The longer-term trend for coffee remained bullish and September was likely to bounce off $1,600 support to test its highs at least once more, they said.
Traders said investors would be unlikely to take any substantial positions before May green coffee stocks data due at 1900 GMT on Monday.
Aggressive shipments by producers were expected to increase stocks by some 150,000-250,000 bags in May, although some estimates were even higher.
Other data being digested by the London and New York markets were the crop estimates released by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) after the New York close on Friday.
The USDA put world and Brazil crops much larger than previous forecasts. Brazil 1997/98 crop was pegged at 28 million 60-kg bags, up from 27.5 million in 1996/97.
World production could reach 103.7 million bags in 1997/98, up from 100.7 million.
Brazilian trade estimates had put next season's crop at anywhere from 18 to 25 million 60-kg bags after this year's yield of at least 27 million.
No damaging frost was forecast for coffee regions in Brazil this week.
In cocoa, technical factors had all turned bullish after second-month September's surge last week to new contract highs.

Traders said they expected more fund, trade and speculative buying to drive September higher to test initial resistance at 1,142 stg, after which there were targets of 1,165 and possibly 1,300 in the longer term.
"There is no doubt funds have been drawn into this (market) but whether they will be right or not, only time will tell," a fund manager said.
Some traders voiced doubts over whether cocoa's blistering rally could be supported by fundamentals.
They said fears that El Nino weather patterns might bring drought to major producers were premature as there had not yet been any concrete evidence that El Nino was affecting crops.
But one trader said statistics had shown a high correlation between El Nino years and those that produced cocoa deficits.
Some traders said talk of early settings for the new Ivory Coast crop were premature. They recalled similar talk a year ago that proved to be wrong.
London's white sugar futures market was expected to remain strong on the normal tightening of supply towards August expiry.
"I think people are fairly encouraged for the moment. They're a little excited towards the upside...London's been reacting very well," said one trader.
But New York's spot July raws would go off the board first on June 30 and would command much attention in the time remaining.
Traders said increased premium buying might occur if London held steady and New York moved lower.
"It will be interesting to see how the August is affected with the arbitrage, if there is suddenly a panic on July," said one.
Fundamentally, traders would continue to monitor the course of Brazilian raw sugar shipments into the Black Sea, where extra duty had been paid on a cargo that was at least partly refined.
